NoteHow the code works

The two blocks use three functions:

normalize(x)                                              # heatmaply
scale(x, center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)                     # base R
describe(x)                                               # psych
  • normalize() applies min-max scaling to each column: it subtracts the minimum and divides by the range, so every column runs from 0 to 1.
  • scale() subtracts each column’s mean and divides by its standard deviation, which gives z-scores with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. It returns a matrix.
  • describe() prints the mean, standard deviation, median, range, skew and kurtosis of each column. The chapter uses it here because summary() does not show the standard deviation.
r <- ggplot(data = ict_derived,
            aes(x = `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue") +
  ggtitle("Raw values without standardisation")

shan_ict_s_df <- as.data.frame(shan_ict.std)
s <- ggplot(data = shan_ict_s_df,
            aes(x = `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue") +
  ggtitle("Min-Max Standardisation")

shan_ict_z_df <- as.data.frame(shan_ict.z)
z <- ggplot(data = shan_ict_z_df,
            aes(x = `RADIO_PR`)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20,
                 color = "black",
                 fill = "light blue") +
  ggtitle("Z-score Standardisation")

ggarrange(r, s, z,
          ncol = 3,
          nrow = 1)
NoteHow the code works
  • The three charts are histograms of the same variable, RADIO_PR, on the three scales. ggtitle() adds a title above each.
  • normalize() returns a data frame but scale() returns a matrix, and ggplot() takes a data frame, so as.data.frame() converts both before plotting.
  • ggarrange() draws the three stored charts in one row.

The chapter’s question is what can be concluded from the three histograms. The shapes are identical. Both methods are linear rescalings, which move and stretch the axis without changing the shape of the distribution. The range changes, and so does the weight of the variable in a Euclidean distance.

The chapter then continues with the raw rates, shan_ict, for every clustering step that follows, and the standardised versions are not used again. The effect of that decision is measured in section 4.2.

NoteHow the scale of a variable affects its weight in the distance

The Euclidean distance between two townships adds up the squared difference on each variable. A variable measured on a wide range produces large differences, and a variable on a narrow range produces small ones, whatever their importance to the question.

3.1.6 Proximity matrix

The clustering in section 3.1.7 groups townships whose ICT rates are close. hclust() takes as its input the distance between every pair of townships, and not the rates themselves, because at each step it compares only distances, first between townships and then between clusters. Computing the distances first, with dist(), sets the kind of distance separately from the clustering, and the same distances are used again for ClustGeo in section 3.3.

proxmat <- dist(shan_ict, method = "euclidean")
as.matrix(proxmat)[1:4, 1:4]
           Mongmit  Pindaya  Ywangan  Pinlaung
Mongmit    0.00000 171.8683 381.8826  57.46286
Pindaya  171.86828   0.0000 257.3161 208.63519
Ywangan  381.88259 257.3161   0.0000 400.05492
Pinlaung  57.46286 208.6352 400.0549   0.00000
NoteHow the code works

The block uses one function:

dist(x, method = "euclidean")                             # stats
  • dist() computes the distance between every pair of rows. With 55 townships there are 55 × 54 / 2 = 1,485 pairs. The result is stored as the lower triangle only, in an object of class dist.
  • as.matrix() converts it to a full square matrix so that a corner of it can be printed. The chapter prints the whole object, which is 1,485 numbers.
NoteWhat the Euclidean distance between two townships measures

The distance is not a distance on the map. Each township is treated as a point whose coordinates are its rates, and the distance is the length of the straight line between two such points, in households per thousand. With two rates the points can be drawn, and the distance is the long side of a right-angled triangle whose other two sides are the differences in the two rates:

\[d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}\]

With all five rates the formula has five squared differences under the square root, one for each rate, and the points can no longer be drawn. For Mongmit and Pindaya the five squared differences give a distance of 171.9, the value printed above.

3.1.7 Hierarchical clustering

Agglomerative hierarchical clustering starts with every township in its own cluster and at each step merges the two closest clusters, until one cluster remains. The methods differ in how they measure the distance between two clusters that each contain several townships. Ward’s method merges the pair whose merger increases the total within-cluster sum of squares by the least.

hclust_ward <- hclust(proxmat, method = "ward.D")
plot(hclust_ward, cex = 0.6)
NoteHow the code works

The block uses two functions:

hclust(d, method = "complete")                            # stats
plot(x, cex)                                              # base R, for hclust objects
  • hclust() runs agglomerative clustering on a dist object. method selects the rule for the distance between clusters. It provides eight, among them "ward.D" and "ward.D2", which give different trees on the same distances.
  • plot() on an hclust object draws the dendrogram. cex = 0.6 shrinks the township labels.
NoteHow agglomerative clustering builds the tree

The procedure is easiest to follow on six points. Each point starts as its own cluster. At each step the two clusters whose merger adds least to the within-cluster sum of squares are joined, which is Ward’s criterion, and the height of the join in the dendrogram records that increase. After five merges one cluster remains. Cutting the tree at a chosen height gives the clusters.

The dashed line cuts the tree below its last merge and leaves two clusters, {A, B, C} and {D, E, F}. The same procedure on the 55 townships gives the dendrogram above, and cutree() makes the cut in section 3.1.12.

3.1.8 Choice of agglomeration method

Ward’s method was used in section 3.1.7 without a comparison. The chapter chooses the method by building a tree with each of four methods, computing the agglomerative coefficient of each tree, and keeping the method with the highest coefficient.

m <- c("average", "single", "complete", "ward")
names(m) <- c("average", "single", "complete", "ward")

ac <- function(x) {
  agnes(shan_ict, method = x)$ac
}

map_dbl(m, ac)
  average    single  complete      ward 
0.8131144 0.6628705 0.8950702 0.9427730
NoteHow the code works

The block uses two functions:

agnes(x, method = "average")                              # cluster
map_dbl(.x, .f)                                           # purrr
  • m is a vector of the four method names. The methods differ in how the distance between two clusters is measured: single linkage uses the closest pair of townships, complete linkage the farthest pair, average linkage the mean over all pairs, and Ward the increase in the within-cluster sum of squares. Slide 11 uses the same three linkages for REDCAP.
  • names(m) <- ... gives each element of m a name, here the same text as its value. map_dbl() copies these names to its result, so each coefficient is printed under the name of its method.
  • ac <- function(x) { ... } defines a new function called ac. function(x) means that it takes one input, called x inside the braces, and the value of the last line in the braces is what it returns. ac("ward") runs agnes(shan_ict, method = "ward").
  • agnes() runs the same kind of agglomerative clustering as hclust(), and computes the Euclidean distances from shan_ict itself. It returns a list, and $ac takes the element called ac from it, the agglomerative coefficient, in the same way as $ takes a column from a table in section 3.1.4.
  • map_dbl(m, ac) calls ac() once for each element of m and collects the four numbers into one named vector. dbl stands for double, R’s type for decimal numbers.

The block gives the same result as the four calls written out:

c(average  = agnes(shan_ict, method = "average")$ac,
  single   = agnes(shan_ict, method = "single")$ac,
  complete = agnes(shan_ict, method = "complete")$ac,
  ward     = agnes(shan_ict, method = "ward")$ac)
NoteWhat the agglomerative coefficient measures

For each township \(i\), agnes() computes the ratio

\[m(i) = \frac{\text{height at which township } i \text{ is first merged}}{\text{height of the final merge}}\]

and the agglomerative coefficient is the average of one minus that ratio over the \(n\) townships (the agnes() documentation; Kaufman and Rousseeuw, 1990):

\[\text{AC} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bigl(1 - m(i)\bigr)\]

A township merged into its group low in the tree has \(m(i)\) close to 0, and \(1 - m(i)\) close to 1.

A coefficient close to 1 therefore means that most townships are in tight groups, and the groups are joined to each other only much higher in the tree. The UC Business Analytics tutorial, the source of this part of the chapter, calls this a strong clustering structure. A lower coefficient means that the merges are spread through the tree, with no clear gap between groups. The two examples have six points each:

The dashed red line is the final merge. In the first example every point is merged into its group far below it. In the second, the merge heights increase steadily up to it.

Ward’s method scores highest, 0.943, and the chapter uses Ward’s method from here on.

3.1.9 Number of clusters

The dendrogram can be cut into any number of clusters, k. The chapter uses the gap statistic to choose k from the data: it compares how tightly the townships are grouped at each k with how tightly data with no clusters would be grouped. The number chosen, six, is used for every set of clusters on the rest of the page.

set.seed(12345)
gap_stat <- clusGap(shan_ict,
                    FUN = hcut,
                    nstart = 25,
                    K.max = 10,
                    B = 50)
print(gap_stat, method = "firstmax")
Clustering Gap statistic ["clusGap"] from call:
clusGap(x = shan_ict, FUNcluster = hcut, K.max = 10, B = 50, nstart = 25)
B=50 simulated reference sets, k = 1..10; spaceH0="scaledPCA"
 --> Number of clusters (method 'firstmax'): 1
          logW   E.logW       gap     SE.sim
 [1,] 8.407129 8.680794 0.2736651 0.04460994
 [2,] 8.130029 8.350712 0.2206824 0.03880130
 [3,] 7.992265 8.202550 0.2102844 0.03362652
 [4,] 7.862224 8.080655 0.2184311 0.03784781
 [5,] 7.756461 7.978022 0.2215615 0.03897071
 [6,] 7.665594 7.887777 0.2221833 0.03973087
 [7,] 7.590919 7.806333 0.2154145 0.04054939
 [8,] 7.526680 7.731619 0.2049390 0.04198644
 [9,] 7.458024 7.660795 0.2027705 0.04421874
[10,] 7.377412 7.593858 0.2164465 0.04540947
fviz_gap_stat(gap_stat)
NoteHow the code works

The two blocks use three functions:

clusGap(x, FUNcluster, K.max, B, ...)                     # cluster
hcut(x, k, hc_method = "ward.D2", ...)                    # factoextra
fviz_gap_stat(gap_stat)                                   # factoextra
  • clusGap() clusters the data for k = 1 to K.max, and for each k also clusters B = 50 reference data sets generated without structure. The gap is the difference between the reference and observed log dispersion. set.seed() fixes the random reference sets so that the result repeats.
  • FUN = hcut makes clusGap() cluster with hcut(), which runs hierarchical clustering and cuts the tree into k groups. Its default method is "ward.D2". nstart = 25 is passed on to hcut(), which does not use it, because nstart is an argument of k-means.
  • print(method = "firstmax") reports the first local maximum of the gap as the recommended k.
  • fviz_gap_stat() plots the gap for each k with an error bar, explained in the callout below. Its dashed line marks the k chosen by its default rule, firstSEmax: the smallest k whose gap is within one standard error of the first peak.

The recommended number is 1. The chapter reads the chart as showing that “the 6-cluster gives the largest gap statistic” and retains six clusters. In the printed table, k = 1 has the largest gap (0.274), and the gap for k = 6 (0.222) is within 0.02 of every other value from k = 2 to 10, while each standard error is about 0.04. This part keeps six clusters, so that the results can be compared with the chapter. The number of clusters on this page is therefore not set by the gap statistic, which is compared with other criteria in section 4.4.

NoteWhat the gap statistic compares

\(W_k\), the within-cluster dispersion, is the sum of the squared distances from each township to the centre of its cluster when the tree is cut into \(k\) clusters. It falls as \(k\) rises, because more clusters always fit the data more closely. clusGap() compares its fall on the data with its fall on 50 reference data sets of the same size, spread evenly over the range of the data, which have no clusters:

\[\text{gap}(k) = \text{average of } \log W_k \text{ over the reference sets} - \log W_k \text{ of the data}\]

The two terms are the two curves below, drawn for the Shan rates. The gap at each \(k\) is the vertical distance between them.

How to read the gap:

  • A smaller \(W_k\) alone means nothing. Adding a cluster always makes \(W_k\) smaller, in the data and in the reference sets alike.
  • A large gap means unusually tight clusters. The townships are much closer to the centres of their clusters than points with no clusters would be.
  • A rise in the gap marks real groups. The gap rises at a \(k\) where the data have groups, and stays flat where an extra cluster only splits the data as it would split random points.
  • The peak gives the number of clusters. A flat gap, as for the Shan rates, gives no clear number.

Why each \(k\) has an error bar:

  • The reference sets are random. Each of the 50 reference data sets gives a slightly different \(\log W_k\), so the gap is an estimate.
  • The bar is one standard error each way. It runs from one standard error below the gap to one above, from the spread of the 50 reference values. The short horizontal lines mark its ends.

How to read the chart of fviz_gap_stat():

  • Each point is the gap at one \(k\), and the line joins the points.
  • A long bar means an uncertain gap.
  • Two bars that overlap belong to gaps that are not clearly different. On the Shan chart all the bars overlap, so no \(k\) is clearly better than another.
  • The dashed vertical line is the \(k\) chosen by the firstSEmax rule.

On the Shan rates the two curves are almost parallel, so the gap hardly changes with \(k\).

Two generic examples, of 90 points each, show the gap with and without clusters, with the same bars as the chart of fviz_gap_stat() above:

With three clear clusters, the gap rises sharply to a peak at \(k = 3\), above the bars of its neighbours, and the first maximum is 3. With points spread evenly, the gap is about the same at every \(k\), within the bars, and the first maximum is \(k = 1\). The Shan rates in the chart above are like the second example.

3.1.10 The dendrogram

The height at which two branches join is the increase in the merging criterion caused by joining them. Two townships are similar if their branches join low in the tree. Their horizontal position is not a measure of similarity.

plot(hclust_ward, cex = 0.6)
rect.hclust(hclust_ward, k = 6, border = 1:6)
NoteHow the code works

The block uses one new function:

rect.hclust(tree, k, border)                              # stats
  • rect.hclust() draws a rectangle around each of the k groups obtained by cutting the tree. border gives the colours. The chapter passes 2:5, four colours for six groups, so two rectangles reuse a colour. 1:6 gives each group its own.

3.1.11 Cluster heatmap

A cluster heatmap draws the data matrix as coloured cells, with the rows ordered by the dendrogram, so that the variables on which each group is high or low can be read across.

shan_ict_mat <- data.matrix(shan_ict)

heatmaply(normalize(shan_ict_mat),
          Colv = NA,
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "ward.D",
          seriate = "OLO",
          colors = Blues,
          k_row = 6,
          margins = c(NA, 200, 60, NA),
          fontsize_row = 4,
          fontsize_col = 5,
          main = "Geographic Segmentation of Shan State by ICT indicators",
          xlab = "ICT Indicators",
          ylab = "Townships of Shan State")
NoteHow the code works

The block uses two functions:

data.matrix(frame)                                        # base R
heatmaply(x, Colv, dist_method, hclust_method, seriate, colors, k_row, ...)  # heatmaply
  • data.matrix() converts the data frame to a numeric matrix, which heatmaply() requires.
  • heatmaply() draws an interactive heatmap, in which hovering over a cell shows its township, variable and value. It clusters the rows itself with dist_method and hclust_method. Colv = NA leaves the columns in their original order. seriate = "OLO" (optimal leaf ordering) reorders the branches so that neighbouring rows are as similar as possible, without changing the tree. k_row = 6 colours six row groups. margins and the font sizes set the layout.

The heatmap clusters normalize(shan_ict_mat), the min-max scaled values, while the dendrogram in section 3.1.10 and the maps in 3.1.12 use the raw values. The six groups on the heatmap are therefore not the six groups on the map.

NoteHow to read the cluster heatmap
  • Each row is one township and each column one rate.
  • The colour of a cell is the township’s rate after min-max scaling (section 3.1.5): white for the lowest value in the state and dark blue for the highest.
  • The rows are in the order of the dendrogram at the left of the heatmap, so rows next to each other are similar townships, and the six coloured branches are the six clusters.
  • Reading across a row gives one township’s profile. Reading down a column within one cluster shows whether the cluster is high or low on that rate.

Seven townships, in the same colours:

Taunggyi, Tachileik and Muse are dark on TV, mobile phone and computer. Pindaya and Ywangan are darkest on radio. Narphan and Matman are light on almost every rate. On the full heatmap, townships with the same pattern are in adjacent rows and form a block of similar colour.

A dark cell, or a value close to 1, means the township is among the highest in the state on that rate; a light cell, or a value close to 0, means the township is among the lowest. For example, Tachileik’s computer cell is the darkest in its column, at 1.00, because Tachileik has the highest computer rate of the 55 townships, 92 households per thousand.

3.1.12 Mapping the clusters

So far the clusters exist only as group numbers in the tree. To see where they are, each township’s group number is attached to its polygon, and the polygons are mapped by group.

groups <- as.factor(cutree(hclust_ward, k = 6))
shan_sf_cluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) |>
  rename(CLUSTER = as.matrix.groups.)
table(shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER)

 1  2  3  4  5  6 
20  4 13  6  7  5
NoteHow the code works

The block uses three functions:

cutree(tree, k)                                           # stats
cbind(...)                                                # base R, sf method
rename(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
  • cutree() cuts the tree at the height that leaves k groups and returns the group number of each township, in the row order of the data. as.factor() makes the numbers categories, so that the map draws them as categories and not as quantities.
  • cbind() binds the group column to shan_sf by row position. This is correct only because shan_ict was built from shan_sf in the same row order. The new column is named as.matrix.groups. after the expression that produced it, and rename() changes the name to CLUSTER.

The same result can be written without the matrix step: shan_sf_cluster <- mutate(shan_sf, CLUSTER = groups).

qtm(shan_sf_cluster, "CLUSTER")
NoteHow the code works
  • qtm() colours each township by its cluster. CLUSTER holds text labels, so qtm() gives each cluster its own colour, with no order between them.

The clusters are fragmented. Cluster 1 appears in the north, the centre and the south, and several clusters are scattered across the state in small pieces. The townships in one cluster are similar in their ICT rates, but a cluster is not one connected region. According to the chapter, the fragmentation is the main limitation of clustering without regard to location. The six clusters are in 24 separate pieces of territory.

3.2 SKATER

SKATER (Spatial ’K’luster Analysis by Tree Edge Removal) was introduced by Assunção et al. (2006). Slides 7 and 8 of the lecture and Assunção et al. (2006, sections 3.3 and 3.4) describe it in four steps:

  1. Represent the townships as nodes of a graph, with an edge between every pair of neighbours.
  2. Give each edge a cost, the dissimilarity between the two townships it joins.
  3. Reduce the graph to a minimum spanning tree: n − 1 edges that connect all n townships at the lowest total cost.
  4. Remove edges from the tree. Each removal splits one branch into two, and each piece that remains is a region. At each step SKATER removes the edge whose removal most reduces the within-region sum of squares.

Because every region is a connected piece of the tree, and every edge of the tree joins two neighbours, every region is contiguous by construction.

3.2.1 Neighbour list

SKATER can only join townships that share a boundary. The neighbour list records, for each township, the townships that touch it, and these pairs become the edges of the graph in step 1.

shan.nb <- poly2nb(shan_sf)
summary(shan.nb)
Neighbour list object:
Number of regions: 55 
Number of nonzero links: 264 
Percentage nonzero weights: 8.727273 
Average number of links: 4.8 
Link number distribution:

 2  3  4  5  6  7  8  9 
 5  9  7 21  4  3  5  1 
5 least connected regions:
3 5 7 9 47 with 2 links
1 most connected region:
8 with 9 links
NoteHow the code works

The block uses one function:

poly2nb(pl, queen = TRUE)                                 # spdep
  • poly2nb() finds, for each polygon, the polygons that share at least one boundary point with it (Queen contiguity, the default). The chapter first converts shan_sf to an sp object with as_Spatial(). The current version of spdep accepts sf objects directly and returns the same list.

The 55 townships have 264 neighbour links, 4.8 per township on average. Every township has at least two neighbours, so no township is isolated and the graph is connected, which SKATER requires.

coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(shan_sf)))

plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), border = grey(0.5))
plot(shan.nb, coords, col = "blue", add = TRUE)
NoteHow the code works

The block uses four functions:

st_geometry(x)                                            # sf
st_centroid(x)                                            # sf
st_coordinates(x)                                         # sf
plot(nb, coords, col, add = TRUE)                         # spdep, for nb objects
  • st_geometry(shan_sf) keeps only the polygons, without the attribute columns. st_centroid() turns each polygon into one point at its centre, and st_coordinates() turns each point into two numbers, its longitude (X) and latitude (Y), one row per township. The figure after this box follows Mongmit through the three functions.
  • The first plot() draws the township boundaries in grey. The second draws a line between the centroids of every pair of neighbours, and add = TRUE draws it on the same plot. The chapter notes that the boundaries go first, because the first call sets the extent of the plot.

The three functions in the first line, applied to one township:

3.2.2 Edge costs

Step 2 gives each edge a cost: the Euclidean distance of section 3.1.6 between the ICT rates of the two townships at its ends, computed only for townships that are neighbours. Neighbours with similar rates have a low cost. The costs are used in section 3.2.3, where the minimum spanning tree is built from the cheapest links.

lcosts <- nbcosts(shan.nb, shan_ict)
shan.w <- nb2listw(shan.nb, lcosts, style = "B")
summary(shan.w)
Characteristics of weights list object:
Neighbour list object:
Number of regions: 55 
Number of nonzero links: 264 
Percentage nonzero weights: 8.727273 
Average number of links: 4.8 
Link number distribution:

 2  3  4  5  6  7  8  9 
 5  9  7 21  4  3  5  1 
5 least connected regions:
3 5 7 9 47 with 2 links
1 most connected region:
8 with 9 links

Weights style: B 
Weights constants summary:
   n   nn       S0       S1        S2
B 55 3025 76267.65 58260785 522016004
NoteHow the code works

The block uses two functions:

nbcosts(nb, data, method = "euclidean")                   # spdep
nb2listw(neighbours, glist = NULL, style = "W")           # spdep
  • nbcosts() computes, for every neighbour link, the same Euclidean distance as dist() in section 3.1.6, on the raw rates in shan_ict. dist() computes it for all 1,485 pairs of townships; nbcosts() only for the pairs that share a boundary.
  • nb2listw() attaches the costs to the neighbour list as weights, and the result, shan.w, is the input mstree() needs in section 3.2.3. style = "B" stores the costs unchanged. The default, "W", would divide each township’s weights by their sum so that they add up to 1, the row standardisation of Exercise 4, and the costs would no longer be distances. This is unrelated to the standardisation of the variables in section 3.1.5.

The link between Exercise 4 and this exercise is the weights object. In Exercise 4 the weight of a link was 1, or 1 divided by the number of neighbours. Here the weight of a link is the dissimilarity between the two townships.

3.2.3 Minimum spanning tree

Step 3 reduces the neighbour links to the 54 that connect all 55 townships at the lowest total cost. The result, the minimum spanning tree, is what SKATER cuts into regions in section 3.2.4.

set.seed(1234)
shan.mst <- mstree(shan.w)
dim(shan.mst)
[1] 54  3
head(shan.mst)
     [,1] [,2]      [,3]
[1,]   28   12  78.78999
[2,]   12   49  59.69478
[3,]   28   13  92.79567
[4,]   13   52 110.55197
[5,]   49   35 124.74445
[6,]   35   37  91.65458
NoteHow the code works

The block uses one function:

mstree(nbw, ini = NULL)                                   # spdep
  • shan.w, from section 3.2.2, is the neighbour list with the cost of each link. mstree() returns shan.mst, a matrix with one row for each link of the tree: the row numbers of the two townships in shan_sf, and the cost of the link.
  • mstree() computes the minimum spanning tree of the weighted graph by Prim’s algorithm: start from one node, and repeatedly add the cheapest edge that connects a node already in the tree to a node not yet in it.
  • The tree has 54 rows, one fewer than the number of townships, because a tree that connects n nodes has n − 1 edges.
  • With ini = NULL, the starting node is chosen at random. The tree itself does not depend on the start when all costs differ, but the order of its rows does, and so does the numbering of the SKATER groups built from it. set.seed() fixes the start so the page gives the same printout on every render. The chapter does not set a seed, so its printout starts from node 54 and this one from a different node.
NoteWhat a minimum spanning tree is

A spanning tree is a set of links that connects every point, directly or through other points, without any loop, so there is exactly one path between any two points. With \(n\) points it always has \(n - 1\) links. A graph has many spanning trees, and the minimum spanning tree is the one whose links have the lowest total cost. The figure uses five points and seven links, with the cost on each link:

SKATER cuts a tree because a tree has no loops: removing any one link splits it into exactly two connected pieces, so every cut in section 3.2.4 adds one region, and every region is contiguous. The minimum spanning tree is made of the links between the most similar neighbours, so the links left for cutting are between townships that are already alike, and a cut separates the most different parts of a branch.

How Prim’s algorithm grows the tree is easiest to see on the same five points. The numbers on the lines are edge costs. Starting from A, the candidates at each step are the edges that join a point already in the tree (blue) to a point outside it (dashed), and the cheapest candidate is added (red):

After four steps all five points are joined by four edges, with a total cost of 10. B was reached last, through its cheapest link to the tree, A-B, and the more expensive links B-C, B-D and B-E were never used. mstree() does the same on the 55 townships, and its output lists the 54 edges in the order they were added, so the first row printed above is the first edge of the tree.

plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), border = gray(0.5))
plot.mst(shan.mst, coords, col = "blue", cex.lab = 0.7, cex.circles = 0.005, add = TRUE)

Each township is now connected to the others by exactly one path. The tree keeps, from the 264 neighbour links, the 54 that join the most similar neighbours while keeping every township connected.

3.2.4 SKATER regions

Step 4 cuts the tree five times, which leaves six regions.

clust6 <- spdep::skater(edges = shan.mst[, 1:2],
                        data = shan_ict,
                        method = "euclidean",
                        ncuts = 5)
ccs6 <- clust6$groups
table(ccs6)
ccs6
 1  2  3  4  5  6 
22 18 11  2  1  1
NoteHow the code works

The block uses one function:

spdep::skater(edges, data, ncuts, crit, vec.crit, method = "euclidean")  # spdep
  • edges is the first two columns of the tree, the pairs of nodes. The costs in column 3 are not passed, because skater() recomputes the within-region sum of squares from data after each cut.
  • ncuts = 5 removes five edges, which leaves six regions. The argument is the number of cuts, one fewer than the number of regions.
  • crit and vec.crit set a minimum size for each region. They are not used in the chapter.
  • The spdep:: prefix selects the spdep version, because rgeoda also has a skater().

The result is a list. $groups holds the region of each township, and $ssto and $ssw hold the total sum of squares and the within-region sum of squares after each cut.

round(clust6$ssw, 0)
[1] 12613 10977  9962  9540  9123  8735

The six regions have 22, 18, 11, 2, 1 and 1 townships, the sizes printed in the chapter. The first cut reduces the within-region sum of squares from 12,613 to 10,977, and each later cut reduces it by less. Two of the six regions are single townships, Ywangan and Narphan.

plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), border = gray(0.5))
plot(clust6, coords, cex.lab = 0.7,
     groups.colors = c("red", "green", "blue", "brown", "pink", "orange"),
     cex.circles = 0.005, add = TRUE)
NoteHow the code works
  • plot() on a skater object draws the pruned tree, with the edges of each region in the colour given for it in groups.colors. The chapter gives five colours for six regions, so the sixth region reuses the first colour. Six colours are given here.
NoteThe four steps of SKATER on Shan

The two maps show steps 1 to 3 listed at the start of section 3.2: the neighbour graph with every Queen link, and the minimum spanning tree with 54 of them.

Each dot is a township and each line an edge.

Step 4 makes the five cuts one at a time. Before each cut, the reduction in the total within-region sum of squares is computed for the removal of every link in every current region, and the link with the largest reduction is removed (slide 8). A cut can therefore fall in any region, and each cut splits one region into two. The six maps show the regions before the first cut and after each cut, with the region split at that cut in colour:

The first cut separates a band of 19 townships in the north and east from the other 36. The second splits the 36 into 24 and 12. The last three cuts each separate one or two townships, which are the small regions in the table in section 3.2.4.

3.2.5 SKATER map

The SKATER regions are attached to the polygons and mapped, beside the hierarchical clusters of section 3.1.12, to compare the two.

groups_mat <- as.matrix(clust6$groups)
shan_sf_spatialcluster <- cbind(shan_sf_cluster, as.factor(groups_mat)) |>
  rename(SP_CLUSTER = as.factor.groups_mat.)
qtm(shan_sf_spatialcluster, "SP_CLUSTER")

The chapter places the two maps side by side.

hclust.map <- qtm(shan_sf_cluster,
                  "CLUSTER") +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)

shclust.map <- qtm(shan_sf_spatialcluster,
                   "SP_CLUSTER") +
  tm_borders(col_alpha = 0.5)

tmap_arrange(hclust.map, shclust.map,
             asp = NA, ncol = 2)
NoteHow the code works
  • cbind() adds the SKATER region of each township to shan_sf_cluster as a new column, and rename() names it SP_CLUSTER, as in section 3.1.12.
  • The chapter writes tm_borders(alpha = 0.5). The reason for col_alpha = 0.5 under tmap 4 is given in section 3.1.2.

The two maps show the difference on slide 5: every SKATER region is one connected piece, and the hierarchical clusters are scattered.

3.3 ClustGeo

ClustGeo (Chavent et al., 2018) adds a second dissimilarity, D1, measured in geographic space, to the dissimilarity D0 in the space of the variables, and minimises a weighted combination of the two. The weight on D1 is the mixing parameter α:

  • at α = 0, only the variables count, and the result is ordinary Ward clustering;
  • at α = 1, only geography counts, and the clusters are compact blocks of territory whatever their ICT rates;
  • in between, a larger α makes the clusters more compact and less homogeneous.

The paper calls this a soft contiguity constraint. Townships that are not neighbours may still end up in the same cluster.

3.3.1 Ward-like clustering without a constraint

With α = 0, ClustGeo is ordinary Ward clustering. Running it first gives the starting point that the geographic constraint then changes.

nongeo_cluster <- hclustgeo(proxmat)
plot(nongeo_cluster, cex = 0.5)
rect.hclust(nongeo_cluster, k = 6, border = 1:6)
NoteHow the code works

The block uses one function:

hclustgeo(D0, D1 = NULL, alpha = 0, scale = TRUE, wt = NULL)  # ClustGeo
  • With only D0, hclustgeo() runs Ward-like clustering on that matrix. D0 must be a dist object.
  • According to Chavent et al. (2018, section 2.2), hclustgeo() is a wrapper of hclust(method = "ward.D") applied to the squared dissimilarities divided by 2n. The chapter describes it as the same as the hclust() call of section 3.1.7. The two produce different trees, because ward.D is applied to unsquared distances in section 3.1.7.
groups <- as.factor(cutree(nongeo_cluster, k = 6))
shan_sf_ngeo_cluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) |>
  rename(CLUSTER = as.matrix.groups.)
qtm(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, "CLUSTER")

The map is as fragmented as the map in section 3.1.12, and the cluster sizes differ from it: 16, 13, 8, 7, 6, 5 here against 20, 13, 7, 6, 5, 4 there.

3.3.2 Geographic distances and the choice of α

ClustGeo needs a second matrix, D1, of geographic dissimilarities, and a value of α. st_distance() supplies D1, and choicealpha() measures, for each α, how much homogeneity in the ICT rates is given up for how much geographic homogeneity.

dist <- st_distance(shan_sf, shan_sf)
distmat <- as.dist(dist)
NoteHow the code works

The block uses two functions:

st_distance(x, y)                                         # sf
as.dist(m)                                                # stats
  • st_distance() returns the matrix of distances between every pair of features. For polygons, the distance is the shortest distance between their boundaries. For longitude and latitude it is computed on the sphere, in metres.
  • as.dist() converts the square matrix to a dist object, as hclustgeo() requires.
  • The chapter names the object dist, the same name as the function dist(). R still finds the function when it is called, because it looks for a function by that name, but the name is easy to misread.

A township and its neighbour touch, so the shortest distance between them is zero.

cr <- choicealpha(proxmat, distmat, range.alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.1), K = 6, graph = TRUE)
NoteHow the code works

The block uses one function:

choicealpha(D0, D1, range.alpha, K, wt = NULL, scale = TRUE, graph = TRUE)  # ClustGeo
  • choicealpha() builds the partition into K clusters for each α in range.alpha, and measures for each partition the proportion of the total pseudo-inertia (a generalised sum of squares) explained in D0 space and in D1 space. graph = TRUE draws both, first as the raw proportions, Q, then as proportions of their own maximum, Qnorm.
round(cbind(cr$Q, cr$Qnorm), 3)
             Q0    Q1 Q0norm Q1norm
alpha=0   0.757 0.131  1.000  0.139
alpha=0.1 0.740 0.284  0.978  0.301
alpha=0.2 0.647 0.626  0.855  0.665
alpha=0.3 0.624 0.692  0.825  0.735
alpha=0.4 0.527 0.831  0.697  0.882
alpha=0.5 0.493 0.874  0.652  0.928
alpha=0.6 0.493 0.874  0.652  0.928
alpha=0.7 0.480 0.879  0.635  0.934
alpha=0.8 0.411 0.940  0.543  0.999
alpha=0.9 0.375 0.918  0.496  0.975
alpha=1   0.191 0.941  0.252  1.000

The chapter uses α = 0.2, read from the charts. Slide 15 of the lecture gives the reasoning with numbers from this data set: at α = 0 the partition explains 0.76 of the ICT variation, and at α = 1 the geographic partition explains 0.94 of the geographic variation. At α = 0.2 the ICT proportion falls by 0.11 to 0.65 and the geographic proportion rises by 0.49 to 0.63. The table printed above gives the same values.

NoteHow to read the choicealpha() charts

Both charts have α on the horizontal axis and one line for each matrix:

  • The black line, Q0, is the share of the variation in the ICT rates (D0) that the six clusters explain. It is highest at α = 0, where only the rates count, and falls as α rises.
  • The red dashed line, Q1, is the share of the geographic variation (D1) that the six clusters explain. It is lowest at α = 0 and rises with α.

Each share is one minus the within-cluster sum of squared dissimilarities divided by the total, the quantity that choicealpha() calls the proportion of explained pseudo-inertia:

\[Q = 1 - \frac{\text{within-cluster sum of squared dissimilarities}}{\text{total sum of squared dissimilarities}}\]

The share of variation explained in Part 2 is the same quantity, computed on the z-scores.

The first chart draws Q0 and Q1 themselves. The second, Qnorm, divides each line by its own maximum, so both lines start from 1 and the two losses can be compared directly. A useful α is one where Q1 has risen a long way while Q0 has fallen only a little. The printed table has the four lines as columns, Q0, Q1, Q0norm and Q1norm, with one row for each α.

3.3.3 ClustGeo regions

With α chosen, the tree is built again from both matrices and cut into six clusters.

clustG <- hclustgeo(proxmat, distmat, alpha = 0.2)
groups <- as.factor(cutree(clustG, k = 6))
shan_sf_Gcluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) |>
  rename(CLUSTER = as.matrix.groups.)
qtm(shan_sf_Gcluster, "CLUSTER")

The clusters are more compact than at α = 0, and several of them are still split. Cluster 4 in this printout, for instance, has townships in the north-west and in the north, a strip in the south-west, and one township in the south-east. The split follows from the soft constraint of Chavent et al. (2018): geography has a weight in the criterion, and a split is still allowed.

NoteWhat the mixing parameter α does

The four maps cut the ClustGeo tree into six clusters at four values of α, with the chapter’s two matrices. At α = 0 the clusters are the same as those of section 3.3.1. As α rises, geography has more weight: the clusters become compact, and at α = 1 they are six blocks of territory formed from distance alone, whatever the ICT rates.

3.4 Cluster profiles

In section 12.10, the clusters are described by their ICT rates. The chapter profiles the non-spatial hclustgeo() clusters of section 3.3.1, and the same clusters are profiled here. The same profile for a set of contiguous regions is in section 4.8.

ggplot(data = shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, aes(x = CLUSTER, y = RADIO_PR)) +
  geom_boxplot()

Each box is the spread of the radio rate across the townships of one cluster, and the line inside it is the median. By median, the clusters rank 3, 2, 1, 4, 6, 5 on radio, the order in the chapter. The chapter calls it the order of the mean, which a boxplot does not show: by mean, the order is 3, 2, 1, 4, 5, 6 (the table of means below).

ggparcoord(data = shan_sf_ngeo_cluster,
           columns = c(17:21),
           scale = "globalminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE,
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of ICT Variables by Cluster") +
  facet_grid(~ CLUSTER) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30))
NoteHow the code works

The two blocks use three new functions:

geom_boxplot()                                            # ggplot2
ggparcoord(data, columns, scale, alphaLines, boxplot, title)  # GGally
facet_grid(rows ~ cols)                                   # ggplot2
  • columns = c(17:21) selects the five rates by position. In shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, columns 17 to 21 are RADIO_PR to COMPUTER_PR, as names(shan_sf) printed in section 2.4 shows.
  • scale = "globalminmax" draws every variable on one common axis without rescaling. Variables with larger values, TV and mobile phone, take up most of the height, and computer is compressed near zero, which reflects the same difference in scale described in section 3.1.5. alphaLines = 0.2 makes the lines transparent, and boxplot = TRUE adds a boxplot on each axis.
  • facet_grid(~ CLUSTER) draws one panel per cluster.
NoteHow to read the parallel coordinate plot

A parallel coordinate plot draws each township as one line. The five rates are five vertical axes side by side, all on the same scale, and a township’s line crosses each axis at the height of its rate. Three townships:

Taunggyi’s line is high on TV and mobile phone. Pindaya’s line is highest on radio and low on mobile phone. Matman’s line is low on every axis. Townships with similar rates have lines of similar shape.

The plot above draws all 55 townships this way, one panel per cluster, with three additions:

  • The lines are transparent, so a dark band is a place where many lines overlap.
  • Each axis has a boxplot of the townships in the cluster: the thick line is the median, the box the middle half of the townships, and a dot a township far from the rest of its cluster.
  • Every panel has the same vertical scale, so the boxes on one axis can be compared across panels by their height.

The boxes from left to right give the typical profile of a cluster, and one axis compared across the panels shows which cluster is high or low on that rate. In panel 4, the TV and mobile phone boxes are the highest of all six panels, with medians of 757 and 655 households per thousand. In panel 5, every box is near the bottom of the scale.

shan_sf_ngeo_cluster |>
  st_set_geometry(NULL) |>
  group_by(CLUSTER) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_RADIO_PR = mean(RADIO_PR),
            mean_TV_PR = mean(TV_PR),
            mean_LLPHONE_PR = mean(LLPHONE_PR),
            mean_MPHONE_PR = mean(MPHONE_PR),
            mean_COMPUTER_PR = mean(COMPUTER_PR)) |>
  kable(digits = 1)
CLUSTER n mean_RADIO_PR mean_TV_PR mean_LLPHONE_PR mean_MPHONE_PR mean_COMPUTER_PR
1 16 220.7 520.9 44.2 245.8 20.5
